'''Evan Michael O'Dorney''' (born September 16, 1993) is an American mathematician who is a [[postdoctoral]] associate at [[Carnegie Mellon University]]. His specialization is [[number theory]]. As a [[home-schooled]] high school student and college student, he won many contests in mathematics and other subjects, including the 2007 [[Scripps National Spelling Bee]], 2011 [[Regeneron Science Talent Search|Intel Science Talent Search]], four [[International Math Olympiad]] medals, and three [[Putnam Fellow]]ships. A 2013 report by the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]] called him "as famous for academic excellence as any student can be".<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7x51AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA142|page=142|title=The Mathematical Sciences in 2025|author=National Research Council, Division on Engineering and Physical Sciences, Board on Mathematical Sciences and Their Applications, Committee on the Mathematical Sciences in 2025|publisher=National Academies Press|year=2013|isbn=9780309284578}}</ref>

==Education and competitions==
O'Dorney grew up in [[Danville, California]]. When he was a child, he was assessed as "'profoundly gifted' with [[autism|autistic]] behaviors", but he has never been formally diagnosed with a [[neurodevelopmental disorder]].<ref name="Chron2024" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5Fc5X2narsc|title= Evan O'Dorney PH.D., 4-Time IMO Medalist, Scripps Spelling Bee Champion, 3-Time Putnam Fellow |website=YouTube |author=Texas Math Mundo|date=April 7, 2023 |access-date=December 1, 2024}}</ref> As a home-schooled high school student, he attended classes at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] from 2007 to 2011. He was the winner of the 2007 [[Scripps National Spelling Bee]];<ref>{{cite news|title=Evan O'Dorney already has formula for success|url=http://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Evan-O-Dorney-already-has-formula-for-success-2528210.php|newspaper=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|first=Jill|last=Tucker|date=March 5, 2011}}</ref> an interview on [[CNN]] with [[Kiran Chetry]] after his win, in which he misspelled ''scombridae'' due to the interviewer's pronunciation, later became a [[viral video]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dailydot.com/entertainment/top-8-spelling-bee-moments-videos/|title=The top 8 moments in Scripps National Spelling Bee history|first=Michelle|last=Jaworski|date=May 31, 2013|website=The Daily Dot}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/education/archive/2015/05/the-spelling-bee-obsession/394394/|magazine=[[The Atlantic (magazine)|The Atlantic]]|date=May 19, 2015|first=Terrance F.|last=Ross|title=The spelling-bee obsession}}</ref> During this time he was a four-time [[International Math Olympiad]] medalist, with two gold and two silver medals.<ref>{{IMO results|id=18028}}</ref> 

In 2010, he won $10,000 (half for himself and half for the Berkeley Mathematics Circle) in a national "Who Wants to Be a Mathematician" contest, held at that year's [[Joint Mathematics Meetings]] in San Francisco.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ams.org/programs/students/wwtbam/jmm2010|title= A National Who Wants to Be a Mathematician at the 2010 Joint Mathematics Meetings|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|access-date=2017-01-22}}</ref> In 2011, he won the top prize in the [[Regeneron Science Talent Search|Intel Science Talent Search]] for a project entitled "continued fraction convergents and linear fractional transformations".<ref>{{cite news|title=Danville's Evan O'Dorney wins Intel Science Talent Search|url=http://www.mercurynews.com/science/ci_17622357?nclick_check=1|newspaper=[[San Jose Mercury News]]|date=2011-03-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Danville HS senior named top winner in Intel competition|url=https://abc7news.com/archive/8015963/|newspaper=ABC7|date=March 15, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=March 17, 2011|url=http://www.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/1103/17/ltm.03.html|title=American Morning: Crisis in Japan; Americans Living Longer Than Ever; SAT Question Stumps Students; America's Next Top Student; Honoring Math & Science|format=transcript}}</ref>

O'Dorney started attending [[Harvard College]] in 2011, where he studied mathematics.<ref name="juggles"/> He enrolled in graduate classes in mathematics, skipping the undergraduate-level classes. While at Harvard, he was a three-time [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|Putnam]] fellow.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.math.harvard.edu/putnam/ | title=Harvard Mathematics Department Putnam Competition | access-date=1 April 2014}}</ref> (His first Putnam was as a high school student.)  After graduating ''summa cum laude'',<ref name=Chron2024>{{cite news |first=Jill |last=Tucker |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/teen-prodigy-evan-odorney-19486219.php |title=He solved a math problem that stumped Stanford profs. Here's what became of a Bay Area prodigy |newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle |date=June 4, 2024 }}</ref> in 2015–16 he studied [[Part III of the Mathematical Tripos]] at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]],<ref>{{cite web|work=Student Stories|url=https://www.chu.cam.ac.uk/news/2015/dec/4/student-stories/|publisher=[[Churchill College, Cambridge]]|date=December 4, 2015|title=Evan O'Dorney: Reading Part III Mathematics}}</ref> on a [[Churchill Scholarship]].<ref name="hzcs"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Danville whiz-kid heads to University of Cambridge as Churchill Scholar|newspaper=[[Chico Enterprise-Record]]|date=February 23, 2015|url=http://www.chicoer.com/article/ZZ/20150223/NEWS/150229056|first=Theresa|last=Harrington}}</ref> In 2016 he received honorable mention for the [[Morgan Prize]] in mathematics. 

In 2021, he earned a PhD in mathematics from [[Princeton University]],<ref name=Chron2024/> with a dissertation titled "Reflection theorems for number rings".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://arks.princeton.edu/ark:/88435/dsp01r207ts47r |title=Reflection theorems for number rings |last=O'Dorney |first=Evan Michael |year=2021 |website=Princeton University Doctoral Dissertations, 2011–2024: Mathematics |access-date=June 8, 2024 }}</ref>

==Career==
He held a two-year post-doctoral position at the [[University of Notre Dame]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://math.nd.edu/people/faculty/evan-odorney |title=Evan O'Dorney |publisher=Department of Mathematics, University of Notre Dame |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230209031629/https://math.nd.edu/people/faculty/evan-odorney/ |archive-date=February 9, 2023 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and then took up a similar appointment at Carnegie Mellon University.<ref name=Chron2024/> His specialization is number theory.<ref name=Chron2024/>

==Other interests==
Although his primary interest is mathematics, O'Dorney has had a strong interest in music. In 2007, he composed a song to help [[Piphilology|memorize the digits]] of [[pi|{{pi}}]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.eastbaytimes.com/2007/07/07/spelling-champ-using-music-to-memorize-pi/|title=Spelling champ using music to memorize pi|first=Jeanine|last=Benca|newspaper=[[East Bay Times]]|date=July 7, 2007}}</ref> At Harvard, he studied music as well as mathematics,<ref name="juggles">{{cite news|url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2012/1/27/Freshman-Math-Profile/?page=single|newspaper=[[The Harvard Crimson]]|date= January 27, 2012|first=Laura K.|last=Reston|title=Freshman O'Dorney Juggles Math and Music}}</ref> and continued to compose music, as well as singing in a chamber music group and playing the organ and piano. He has [[absolute pitch]].<ref name="hzcs">{{cite news|url=http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2015/03/senior-named-churchill-scholar/|title=Senior named Churchill Scholar|newspaper=Harvard Gazette|date=March 30, 2015|first=Stephanie|last=Kacoyanis}}</ref> O’Dorney finds spirituality in his mathematical studies, and his meeting with Eric Riedl at a Catholic Mass led him to Notre Dame.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tadavarthy |first=Naya |title=Evan O'Dorney finds beauty in faith and math |url=https://science.nd.edu/news-and-media/news/evan-odorney-finds-beauty-in-faith-and-math/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240818035254/https://science.nd.edu/news-and-media/news/evan-odorney-finds-beauty-in-faith-and-math/ |archive-date=2024-08-18 |access-date=2025-03-27 |website=College of Science |language=en-US}}</ref>
